How does life expectancy change over time for each continent?

The challenge:

Life expectancy for a country is the mean length of life over the people of that country. Using the variables life expectancy (lifeExp) and population (pop) of a country, from the gapminder dataset:

  1. Derive a formula to compute the life expectancy of a continent (a group of countries).
  2. Plot how life expectancy changed over time for each continent.
  3. Do the same for the whole planet.
gapminder
## # A tibble: 1,704 × 6
##    country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
##    <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
##  1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
##  2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
##  3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
##  4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
##  5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
##  6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.
##  7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.
##  8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.
##  9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.
## 10 Afghanistan Asia       1997    41.8 22227415      635.
## # ℹ 1,694 more rows

Each row is one country in one year, with its lifeExp and pop already recorded. There is no lifeExp column for a continent or for the world, we have to build one ourselves.

1 Part 1: deriving the formula

1.1 Why a simple average across countries is wrong

The naive approach is to just average lifeExp across all countries in a continent for a given year:

\[ L_{\text{naive}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} L_i \]

This treats every country equally, no matter whether it has 1 million or 1 billion people. We can see this bias directly in the data: a tiny country gets exactly the same weight as a population giant.

gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia") %>%
  select(country, pop, lifeExp) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop))
## # A tibble: 33 × 3
##    country            pop lifeExp
##    <fct>            <int>   <dbl>
##  1 China       1318683096    73.0
##  2 India       1110396331    64.7
##  3 Indonesia    223547000    70.6
##  4 Pakistan     169270617    65.5
##  5 Bangladesh   150448339    64.1
##  6 Japan        127467972    82.6
##  7 Philippines   91077287    71.7
##  8 Vietnam       85262356    74.2
##  9 Iran          69453570    71.0
## 10 Thailand      65068149    70.6
## # ℹ 23 more rows

China and India alone hold the overwhelming majority of Asia’s population in this table, yet a plain average of the lifeExp column would let Bahrain or Bhutan move the “continent average” just as much as China does. That can’t be right if we want a number that reflects how long the typical person on that continent lives.

1.2 The correct formula: a population-weighted mean

Life expectancy is a rate (years per person); population is an extensive quantity (a count of people). To combine a rate correctly across groups of different sizes, each country’s lifeExp must be weighted by its share of the continent’s total population:

\[ L_{\text{continent}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i \, L_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i} \]

This is not an ad hoc fix, it falls directly out of what life expectancy means. If \(L_i\) is the average lifespan of the \(P_i\) people in country \(i\), then \(P_i L_i\) is the total number of life-years lived in that country. Summing \(P_i L_i\) over every country in the continent and dividing by the continent’s total population gives the average lifespan across every individual on the continent, regardless of which country they live in, exactly \(L_{\text{continent}}\) above. The same formula, applied over every country in the world instead of just one continent, gives the population-weighted life expectancy of the whole planet.

We implement this with a single group_by() + summarise():

weighted_lifeexp <- function(lifeExp, pop) {
  sum(lifeExp * pop) / sum(pop)
}

2 Part 2: life expectancy over time, by continent

continent_lifeexp <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(
    lifeExp_weighted = weighted_lifeexp(lifeExp, pop),
    lifeExp_naive     = mean(lifeExp),
    pop_total         = sum(pop)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

continent_lifeexp
## # A tibble: 60 × 5
##    continent  year lifeExp_weighted lifeExp_naive pop_total

##  1 Africa     1952             38.8          39.1 237640501
##  2 Africa     1957             40.9          41.3 264837738
##  3 Africa     1962             43.1          43.3 296516865
##  4 Africa     1967             45.2          45.3 335289489
##  5 Africa     1972             47.2          47.5 379879541
##  6 Africa     1977             49.2          49.6 433061021
##  7 Africa     1982             51.0          51.6 499348587
##  8 Africa     1987             52.8          53.3 574834110
##  9 Africa     1992             53.4          53.6 659081517
## 10 Africa     1997             53.3          53.6 743832984
## # ℹ 50 more rows

2.1 The main plot

ggplot(continent_lifeexp, aes(year, lifeExp_weighted, color = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Population-weighted life expectancy by continent, 1952–2007",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Life expectancy (years)",
    color = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The plot shows the pattern we’d expect from first principles: every continent trends upward over time, but Africa starts far below the others and the gap between continents narrows over the decades (convergence), rather than all the lines staying parallel.

2.2 Does weighting actually matter here?

We can check this directly by comparing the naive (unweighted) average to the population-weighted one, continent by continent:

continent_lifeexp %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(lifeExp_weighted, lifeExp_naive),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "lifeExp"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, lifeExp, color = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ continent) +
  labs(
    title = "Weighted vs. naive (unweighted) continent life expectancy",
    x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The two methods diverge most on continents made of countries with very unequal populations (Asia, dominated by China and India; the Americas, dominated by the US and Brazil), and they’re closest where countries are more similar in size. This confirms the reasoning from Part 1: weighting only matters when population is unevenly distributed across the group being aggregated.

2.3 A closer look: dips and shocks

Following the same approach as the “many simple models” case study, fitting a linear trend of lifeExp against year for each country and inspecting the residuals, reveals where the continent-level dips actually come from:

country_models <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(country, continent) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ lm(lifeExp ~ year, data = .x)),
    data  = map2(data, model, ~ add_residuals(.x, .y))
  ) %>%
  unnest(data)

ggplot(country_models, aes(year, resid, group = country)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ continent) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals of lifeExp ~ year, by country, faceted by continent",
    x = "Year", y = "Residual (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Africa stands out from every other continent: several countries show a sharp mid-series collapse away from a simple linear improvement. This is the HIV/AIDS mortality shock of the 1990s, and because it hit several populous African countries at once, it is exactly the kind of event that shows up as a visible dent in the population-weighted continent curve above, even though it affected only one continent.

3 Part 3: the same formula for the whole planet

The planet is simply the special case of “one continent” containing every country on Earth. The identical weighted-mean formula applies, we just drop continent from the grouping:

world_lifeexp <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    lifeExp_weighted = weighted_lifeexp(lifeExp, pop),
    pop_total         = sum(pop)
  )

world_lifeexp
## # A tibble: 12 × 3
##     year lifeExp_weighted  pop_total
##    <int>            <dbl>      <dbl>
##  1  1952             48.9 2406957150
##  2  1957             52.1 2664404580
##  3  1962             52.3 2899782974
##  4  1967             57.0 3217478384
##  5  1972             59.5 3576977158
##  6  1977             61.2 3930045807
##  7  1982             62.9 4289436840
##  8  1987             64.4 4691477418
##  9  1992             65.6 5110710260
## 10  1997             66.8 5515204472
## 11  2002             67.8 5886977579
## 12  2007             68.9 6251013179
ggplot(world_lifeexp, aes(year, lifeExp_weighted)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "black") +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Population-weighted world life expectancy, 1952–2007",
    x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

3.1 Checking internal consistency: country-level vs. continent-level aggregation

The weighted-mean formula has a useful consistency property (a form of the law of total expectation): we should get the same world average whether we aggregate directly over every country, or aggregate continents first and then combine those continent totals. Let’s verify this numerically:

world_from_continents <- continent_lifeexp %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(lifeExp_from_continents = weighted_lifeexp(lifeExp_weighted, pop_total))

world_lifeexp %>%
  left_join(world_from_continents, by = "year") %>%
  mutate(difference = lifeExp_weighted - lifeExp_from_continents)
## # A tibble: 12 × 5
##     year lifeExp_weighted  pop_total lifeExp_from_continents difference
##    <int>            <dbl>      <dbl>                   <dbl>      <dbl>
##  1  1952             48.9 2406957150                    48.9   0       
##  2  1957             52.1 2664404580                    52.1   0       
##  3  1962             52.3 2899782974                    52.3   0       
##  4  1967             57.0 3217478384                    57.0   0       
##  5  1972             59.5 3576977158                    59.5  -7.11e-15
##  6  1977             61.2 3930045807                    61.2   0       
##  7  1982             62.9 4289436840                    62.9   0       
##  8  1987             64.4 4691477418                    64.4   0       
##  9  1992             65.6 5110710260                    65.6   0       
## 10  1997             66.8 5515204472                    66.8   0       
## 11  2002             67.8 5886977579                    67.8   0       
## 12  2007             68.9 6251013179                    68.9   0

The difference column is (up to floating-point rounding) zero for every year: aggregating country \(\to\) world directly and aggregating country \(\to\) continent \(\to\) world give identical results, exactly as the formula predicts.

3.2 Comparing the world curve to the continents

continent_lifeexp %>%
  select(continent, year, lifeExp_weighted) %>%
  bind_rows(
    world_lifeexp %>% mutate(continent = "World") %>%
      select(continent, year, lifeExp_weighted)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, lifeExp_weighted, color = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "World life expectancy vs. each continent",
    x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)", color = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

As expected, the world curve sits between the continent curves, pulled closest to Asia and the Americas, the continents holding the largest shares of world population, and it shows the same long-run upward trend as the continents individually, smoothed because a shock confined to one continent is diluted by the rest of the world’s population when averaged globally.

4 Conclusion

  1. Life expectancy must be aggregated with population as weights, \(L_{\text{continent}} = \dfrac{\sum_i P_i L_i}{\sum_i P_i}\), not with a plain average, because life expectancy is a per-person rate and countries differ hugely in how many people that rate applies to.
  2. Computing this for each continent and year shows a long-run upward trend, convergence between continents, and a sharp dip in Africa in the 1990s driven by HIV/AIDS, visible in the residuals of simple per-country linear models.
  3. The identical formula, applied over every country on Earth, gives the world’s life expectancy, and this is numerically consistent whether computed directly from countries or in two steps through continents, confirming the formula is internally coherent across levels of aggregation.
